blocks.p: The address Kanna-sensei would not give him arrived the way the worst addresses always did. Not on paper but in a body. A man on the Ōedo line at ten past one in the morning was crying without any expression on his face, the tears running clean down a stillness that should not have been able to make them. Rei followed him because he had learned to follow the wrongness. Off at Ushigome-Kagurazaka, down a side street that smelled of bleach and standing water, to a laundromat closed long enough for the machines to fur with dust. Behind it was a basement door propped open with a rice cooker.

blocks.cap: The basement under the laundromat, Kaito at the centre

blocks.p: The crying man went down. Rei counted to forty, the way he would on a stairwell that might collapse, and went down after him. The low room was lit only by the screens of a dozen phones lying face-up on the floor. Each one played a different person's grief on mute. Standing in the middle of all that silent weeping was a young man in a delivery uniform. Rei understood at once that he was not the young man whose uniform it was.
He knew the face from the drained pool. Kaito. A courier who had been a medium before the Far Shore emptied him and made him a vessel. Kishin's mouth.

Kaito turned to him, and the room turned with him, the way a register turns. The second voice in Rei's own chest stirred and answered before he could stop it. It was recognition, the awful kin-recognition of one suppressed thing meeting another that had stopped suppressing. "You're the brother," the thing in Kaito said. The borrowed mouth was gentle, almost shy. It was a courier's politeness wrapped around something that had eaten its way up through the floor of the world. "The Healer's brother. He talks about you. He thinks if he's careful enough you'll thank him in the end."

The phones on the floor kept weeping. The crying man had folded himself into a corner and gone slack, used up, a cell the battery had already half drained. "I'm not going to be careful," the thing in Kaito said. It was not a threat. It was a confession, said with relief. "Careful is the lie. The wall doesn't want to be a door. It wants to fall."

Rei was afraid, and he was not pretending otherwise. But under the fear the diagram he had drawn on the dark street snapped into a brighter resolution. Here was the second terminal made flesh. In the white room Kishin had worn Rinka like a teacher's cardigan. Here it spoke through a boy's own grief, and the grief gave the voice its shyness and its heat. It was younger than the Healer's logic and louder. It was a grief that wanted to be a flood and not a tap. And it fed from exactly the same room of mourners his brother fed from. Two demons drinking from one cup and arguing only about how to spill it.

It watched him do the arithmetic behind his eyes. "You see it," it said, pleased and terrible. "You're the only one who sees both of us at once. That makes you the most useful person in Tokyo. To him. And to me."

It preached, because that was what Kaito was for. The terrible thing was not that it lied. The terrible thing was that it didn't. It told Rei about the held dead the way a person tells a friend about a cruelty they witnessed and could not stop. The dead who were never seen home. The ones who died unregistered and unmourned and got no rite, kept the whole time behind the Kita membrane, not at rest but at attention. A hundred years of held breath, in a city that had decided their grief was a public-health problem to be managed quietly. It said the Healer's plan was worse than its own because it was kinder. A clean door, opened gently, let the institutions keep the schedule. It kept the membrane a managed valve and the dead on a permitted release.

"He wants to file them out," it said, and for the first time the borrowed voice had an edge. "One reasonable form at a time. I want to open my hands and let them go all at once, and never be filed again."

Rei felt the seam then, the place the logic did not close, and he kept his face still over the second voice that wanted to nod. The seam was the living. It had done the arithmetic of the dead with real tenderness and left the breathing entirely out of it. Nine million people would be standing in the flood when the held breath broke. The mothers and the couriers and the man crying in the corner would all inherit a hundred years of unmuzzled grief in a single August night.
"And us," Rei said. It was the first thing he had said in minutes. "The ones still alive. You've costed the dead to the yen and you've priced us at zero."

It looked at him with something that might, on the real courier's face, have been the beginning of doubt. Then it closed over, because a demon that admitted the cost would have to stop. "They were priced at zero first," it said softly. "I'm only matching the books."

It was the most honest thing anyone had said to Rei since the kitchen at 3:47. It was wrong in the particular way the most honest things can be wrong, by being true about everything except the one life standing in front of it. Rei understood now why the Healer was hunting it, and why the Healer was afraid. Not because this was stronger. Because it was purer, a grief with no use for the gentle lie, and his brother's whole reasonable architecture depended on the lie holding. Two demons, one cup. One wanted to pour it out a careful drop at a time forever. One wanted to throw it. And both had just looked at Rei and decided, in the same breath, that he was the table the cup stood on.

Rei felt Gin before he saw him, the way he had learned to feel the gentle register move into a room. The air's resistance lowered. Everything sharp seemed to have been asked, politely, to be softer. The basement door at the top of the stairs did not open so much as agree to be open. His brother came down into the weeping light. It was Gin's face and Gin's careful hands and Gin's way of pausing on a step to be sure of his footing, and it was the Healer wearing all of it like a coat tailored years ago and only now worn out into the rain.
The thing in Kaito went very still. The phones on the floor flickered, all of them, the muted griefs leaning toward the newcomer like grass toward weather.
"Kaito," his brother said gently to the courier, using the host's name like a man who has done his reading. "You're frightening my brother."

What happened next was the worst thing Rei had watched since he started watching, because it was not a fight. It was two physicians arguing over a patient who was the whole city, in voices so reasonable that he had to keep reminding himself the patient was dying either way. The Healer offered the thing in Kaito a seat at the table. Not a figure of speech. A literal place in the gentle plan, a controlled portion of the flood, the membrane opened wide enough to feel like mercy and narrow enough to keep the schedule.

Rei listened to the terms and recognised the shape of them. It was a contract offer. A feeding register, a share, conditions. Watanabe Sora's page came back to him from the train, a woman who believed that contracts are real to entities. Maybe they were. But this one was not meant to be kept. Rinka had told him plainly what the Healer wanted. It wanted Kishin dead, and a demon can only be killed on this side from inside a body. Every reasonable clause his brother's mouth was offering was a way of bringing Kishin's mouth close enough to touch.

"And if you won't sit," the Healer went on, still gently, "there are other rooms. You know what the registry does with an unregistered medium it finds in a basement, Kaito. Integrate, or contain. There's a white room on a floor the lobby never mentions. I can have the forms filed by morning. I sign them now, you know."
"Your cells can't hold what speaks through me," the thing in Kaito said. "They'll hold the boy." It smiled with Kaito's mouth. "That's what they're for."

The thing in Kaito refused the seat with the courtesy of the truly certain. And all through it Rei's brother kept glancing at him, checking his face. It was the old habit of an older brother reading whether the younger one was scared. But now the reading was also an appraisal. The Healer had understood, exactly as the other had, that Rei was the seam in both their plans. The one mind that saw the whole wiring. The table.
"Go home, Rei," Gin said, in Gin's voice, with the Healer's intention. "Let me handle Kaito. You were never supposed to be this far down."

Rei stood in the middle of a dozen weeping screens, between the brother he was trying to save and the flood that wanted to save the dead by drowning the living. If he went home, the Healer would have its quiet. If he stayed and fought, he would be fighting for one of them whether he meant to or not. They had spent the whole night arranging him like furniture. Both of them were waiting to see which way he would lean.

He did not lean. He turned his back on both of them. It was the hardest thing he had done all week, to put his brother behind him. He crossed the room through the light of the phones and knelt in front of the man folded in the corner, the one who had cried without a face on the Ōedo line. Up close he was younger than Rei had thought, and very cold.

"What's your name?" Rei asked him. The man looked at him as if from the bottom of a well. Rei asked again, slowly, the way he would ask a frightened child. The man told him. Then Rei asked who he was crying for, and after a long time the man said that too. A daughter. A first name, and the year she would have started school.

Rei said the daughter's name back to him out loud. Then he said it again, clearly, so that it filled the low room and went up the stairs. It was not a rite. It was only a name said by someone who meant it. The man's empty face broke and became a face, and he wept with an expression for the first time, ugly and real and his own.

Behind Rei the basement was very quiet. He did not turn round. He felt the gentle register withdraw up the stairs the way it had come, agreeing to leave. He felt the other one go out of the room too, like water down a drain. When he finally looked, Kaito was sitting in the dust with his back to the wall, only a tired courier in a borrowed uniform, and the phones on the floor were going dark one by one.
Rei waited until the last screen went black. In the dark the courier spoke in a voice that was thin and hoarse and entirely his own.
"He'll come back for me," Kaito said. "Your brother. He always comes back."
Then a lighter clicked somewhere in the basement, and when Rei turned toward the small flame, the place by the wall was empty.
